title: Simulating the rules
objectives: Turn a long rule statement into a correct simulation, as online assessments often ask.

screens.title: Read it, then trace it
screens.prose: Online assessments often state a long rule and ask you to simulate it. This is one, with prices in whole pence. Trace it by hand on six days before writing any code.

params.title: The statement
lines: A bot trades one unit of one stock. Prices are whole pence.
It starts flat. Day 0 never trades.
While flat on day i >= 1, it buys at that day's price
when the price is below the previous day's price.
While long, it checks three rules on each later day, in order:
1. Sell if 100 * p >= 105 * entry (at least 5% up).
2. Sell if 100 * p <= 97 * entry (at least 3% down).
3. Sell if i - bought == 3 (held exactly 3 days).
A bot that sells on day i does not buy on day i.
If it still holds at the end, it sells at the last price.
Return [total profit in pence, number of trades].

screens.question: What total profit, in pence, does the bot make on these six days?

widget.label: Profit
widget.accept: 6: buy at 98 on day 1, sell at 104 on day 4

hints.text: On which day is the price first below the day before?
Day 1 buys at 98. Now test each later day against $105 \times 98 = 10{,}290$ and $97 \times 98 = 9{,}506$.
Day 4: $100 \times 104 = 10{,}400 \ge 10{,}290$, so it sells at 104. Profit $104 - 98 = 6$. Day 5 does not buy.

feedback.correct: Buy at 98 on day 1, sell at 104 on day 4: 6 pence.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace one day at a time and check the rules in order.

byKey.held: You held to the last price, 110. Rule 1 fires first on day 4, at 104.
byKey.day0: You bought on day 0. Day 0 never trades; the first buy is day 1 at 98.
byKey.none: You found no trade. Day 1's 98 is below day 0's 100, so the bot buys.

explain.text: Day 1 buys at 98 because 98 is below 100. Day 4 is the first day with $100p \ge 105 \times 98$, so it sells at 104. Day 5 is flat and 110 is not a fall, so the result is `[6, 1]`.

screens.title: One day at a time
screens.prose: Step through the days with the slider. The caption shows each check the bot makes. Then fill in the position at each close: 1 when long, 0 when flat.

derive.caption: {{["Day 0: never trades. Flat.", "Day 1: 98 is below 100, so buy at 98. Long.", "Day 2: 9,900 is under 10,290 and over 9,506; held 1 day. Long.", "Day 3: 10,000 is under 10,290 and over 9,506; held 2 days. Long.", "Day 4: 10,400 is at least 10,290, so sell at 104. Flat.", "Day 5: flat, and 110 is not below 104. Flat."][d]}}

screens.question: Fill in the position at the close of each day.

hints.text: The bot is long from the day it buys to the day it sells.
It buys on day 1 and sells on day 4.
Days 1, 2 and 3 close long (1). Days 4 and 5 close flat (0).

feedback.correct: Long at the close of days 1 to 3, flat on days 4 and 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step the slider to each day and read the caption.

byKey.r1c2: Day 1 buys at 98, so the bot is long at the close.
byKey.r4c2: Day 4 sells at 104, so the bot is flat at the close.
byKey.r5c2: Day 5 is flat: 110 is not below 104, so it does not buy.

explain.text: The state between days is three values: long or flat, the entry price and the buy day. Each day is one event that may change them. That is all the simulation has to remember.

canvas.caption: Day 4: 10,400 is at least 10,290, so sell at 104. Flat.

screens.title: Two rules at once
screens.prose: Now the prices are `[100, 98, 99, 100, 103]`. The bot buys at 98 on day 1. On day 4, $100 \times 103 = 10{,}300 \ge 10{,}290$, and the bot has held for exactly 3 days.

state.caption: Day 4: rule 1 and rule 3 are both true

screens.question: Which rule sells the bot on day 4?

options.text: Rule 1, the take profit, because it is checked first
Rule 3, the time rule, because 3 days have passed
options.why: Rule 3 is true too, but the statement checks rule 1 first, and only one sale happens.

options.text: Both: it sells twice
options.why: The bot holds one unit. The first rule that fires sells it, and the others are not checked.

options.text: Neither: two true rules cancel out
options.why: Rules do not cancel. The first true rule in order sells the bot.

hints.text: Read the statement: in what order are the rules checked?
Rule 1 is checked first, and it is true.
The first true rule wins. Rule 1 is true, so it sells; rule 3 is never reached.

feedback.correct: Rule 1 fires first. The price is the same, but the reason is take profit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The statement fixes the order of the checks.

byKey.b: You picked the rule you noticed first. The statement checks rule 1 before rule 3.
byKey.c: You sold twice. One unit can be sold once, by the first rule that fires.
byKey.d: You let the rules cancel. In order, the first true one sells.

explain.text: Here both rules sell at 103, so the profit is the same. A log of reasons, or a rule that sells at a different price, would differ. Write the checks in the order the statement gives, as one `if ... or ... or ...`.

screens.title: Counting days held
screens.prose: Rule 3 reads `i - bought == 3`. Here the bot buys at 99 on day 2, and neither price rule fires afterwards.
screens.question: On which day does rule 3 sell the bot?

hints.text: Rule 3 needs `i - bought` to equal 3.
`bought` is 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve `i - bought == 3` with `bought = 2`.

byKey.early: You counted the buy day as the first day held. `i - bought` is 2 on day 4.
byKey.late: You waited for more than 3 days. The rule is `== 3`, so it fires on day 5.

explain.text: Days held is `i - bought`, which is 1 on day 3, 2 on day 4 and 3 on day 5. So rule 3 sells at 100 on day 5. Writing `> 3` instead would sell a day late.

screens.title: Write the simulation
screens.prose: Keep three variables of state: `long_`, `entry` and `bought`. Each day, a flat bot may buy and a long bot checks the rules in order. An `if ... else` on `long_` stops a bot from buying on the day it sold.

params.title: The statement
lines: A bot trades one unit of one stock. Prices are whole pence.
It starts flat. Day 0 never trades.
While flat on day i >= 1, it buys at that day's price
when the price is below the previous day's price.
While long, it checks three rules on each later day, in order:
1. Sell if 100 * p >= 105 * entry (at least 5% up).
2. Sell if 100 * p <= 97 * entry (at least 3% down).
3. Sell if i - bought == 3 (held exactly 3 days).
A bot that sells on day i does not buy on day i.
If it still holds at the end, it sells at the last price.
Return [total profit in pence, number of trades].

screens.question: Write `run_strategy(prices)`: apply the statement and return `[profit, trades]`. `prices` may be empty.

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests, including a list of one price and an empty list. Results are compared with `==`.

hints.text: What must the bot remember from one day to the next?
Whether it is long, the entry price and the buy day.
Loop with `enumerate`. If flat, buy when `i >= 1` and `p < prices[i - 1]`. Else sell on any of the three rules. After the loop, sell a holding at `prices[-1]`.

feedback.correct: State, one event per day, the checks in order, and the end rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is the hook. Buy at 98 on day 1 and sell at 104 on day 4.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 never falls, so the bot never trades: `[0, 0]`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 falls every day. Buy 99, sell 96 on day 4, buy 95 on day 5, sell 93 at the end: `[-5, 2]`.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 has one price. Day 0 never trades, so the answer is `[0, 0]`.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 is an empty list. Only read `prices[-1]` when the bot still holds.

explain.text: The `else` branch means a bot that sells today waits until tomorrow to buy. The end rule runs only when `long_` is still true, so an empty list never reads `prices[-1]`. Integer arithmetic keeps the 5% and 3% tests exact.

screens.title: Selling and buying on one day
screens.prose: Prices `[100, 95, 90, 85]`. The bot buys at 95 on day 1. On day 2, $9{,}000 \le 97 \times 95 = 9{,}215$, so the stop sells at 90. Day 2's price is also below day 1's.

state.caption: Day 2: the stop fires, and 90 is below 95

screens.question: What does `run_strategy([100, 95, 90, 85])` return?

options.why: You let the bot buy at 90 on the day it sold. The statement forbids that, so it waits until day 3.
You stopped after the first sale. Day 3's 85 is below 90, so the bot buys again and sells at the end.
You held from 100 to 85. Day 0 never trades, and the stop sells on day 2.

hints.text: What does the statement say about the day the bot sells?
On day 2 the bot sells, so it may not buy on day 2.
Day 3: flat, and 85 is below 90, so it buys at 85 and sells at the end at 85. Total $-5 + 0$, two trades.

feedback.correct: Stop at 90 on day 2, buy 85 on day 3, sell 85 at the end: `[-5, 2]`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace day 2 and day 3 again with the same-day rule.

byKey.b: You let the bot buy on the day it sold. Then it buys 90, is stopped at 85 on day 3, and buys again.
byKey.c: You forgot the buy on day 3. A flat bot buys whenever the price falls, after the day of a sale.
byKey.d: You bought on day 0 and held. Day 0 never trades.

explain.text: With the same-day buy, day 2 buys 90, day 3 stops at 85 and buys 85 again: `[-10, 3]`. The statement forbids the buy on day 2, so day 3 buys 85 and the end sells it for 0. The `else` on `long_` is what enforces it.

screens.title: How to read a long statement
screens.prose:
Every simulation question has the same three parts.

```python
state = ...            # what is remembered between steps
for event in events:   # what arrives each step
    state = step(state, event)  # checks in the stated order
finish(state)          # the end-of-data rule
```
screens.question: Put the steps of reading a long statement in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: Read the whole statement once without coding
List the state: long or flat, entry price, buy day
List the events: one price per day
Write the checks in the stated order, with the same-day and end rules
Trace a short list by hand and write down the expected result
Code one step per event, then run it on your trace
Code rule 1 while reading the rest of the statement
lines.why: Rules later in the statement change earlier ones, such as the same-day rule. Read it all first.

hints.text: What do you need before you can write the checks?
The state and the events come before the order of checks.
Read, state, events, order, hand trace, then code. Leave out coding while reading.

feedback.correct: Read, state, events, order, trace, code.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs the one before it.

byKey.d1: You started coding while reading. The same-day rule, near the end, changes how rule 1's sale behaves.
byKey.left-out: Every step but one belongs. Only coding while reading is wrong.

explain.text: The state and events fix the shape of the loop. The order of checks and the edge rules fill in its body. A hand trace gives you expected values before any code exists.

screens.title: Prices from a file
screens.prose: The assessment now gives the prices as a CSV file with columns `day` and `price_pence`. Three files sit in the working directory. Open the Data files panel to see them. `run_strategy` is done; write only the reader.

params.title: ticks-3.csv
lines: day,price_pence

screens.question: Write `load_prices(path)`: return the `price_pence` column as a list of `int`, in file order.

widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests, one per file: 40 days, 3 days, and a header with no rows.

hints.text: Which module reads a CSV with a header row?
`csv.DictReader` gives each row as a dictionary keyed by the header.
`with open(path) as f: return [int(row['price_pence']) for row in csv.DictReader(f)]`.

feedback.correct: The reader turns each row into an `int` and keeps the order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 reads `ticks-40.csv`. Skip the header and convert each price with `int`.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 reads `ticks-3.csv`: prices 10,000, 9,900 and 10,600, so the result is `[700, 1]`.

explain.text: `DictReader` uses the first line as the keys, so the header is never a price. A file with only the header gives `[]`, and `run_strategy([])` returns `[0, 0]`. On `ticks-3.csv` the bot buys 9,900 on day 1 and sells 10,600 on day 2.

screens.title: Before you code, ask
screens.prose: A desk analyst writes three versions of the time rule for a bot. You can ask one question before coding.

params.title: Three specs
lines: A: It sells after three days.
B: It sells on the third day after the buy day.
C: It sells on day i when i - bought == 3.

screens.question: Which spec is ambiguous, and what do you ask?

options.text: A: ask whether it sells on day `bought + 3` or later
B: ask whether the buy day itself counts as day 1
options.why: B counts days after the buy day, so day `bought + 3`. That is the same as C.

options.text: C: ask what `bought` means
options.why: C names the variable and the test exactly. It is the clearest of the three.

options.text: None: all three say the same thing
options.why: A can be read as `== 3` or as `> 3`. Those sell on different days.

hints.text: Which spec could be coded in two ways?
"After three days" could mean once three days have passed, or later than that.
A could be `== 3` or `> 3`. Ask which day it sells on.

feedback.correct: A could mean `== 3` or `> 3`; the question settles the day.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a spec that two programmers could code differently.

byKey.b: You doubted B. Counting days after the buy day gives `bought + 3`, the same as C.
byKey.c: You doubted C. It states the test in code, so it has one reading.
byKey.d: You read A one way only. "After three days" can also mean the fourth day.

explain.text: A can be coded as `i - bought == 3` or `i - bought > 3`, which sell a day apart. B and C both mean day `bought + 3`. One question before coding saves a rewrite after a failing test.

screens.title: A week on the desk
screens.prose: The desk runs the bot on last week's closes, in pence: `[250, 240, 245, 252, 249, 247, 236, 240]`. On day 3, $100 \times 252 = 25{,}200$, exactly $105 \times 240$.
screens.question: What total profit, in pence, does the bot make?

widget.label: Profit
widget.accept: −1: $+12$ on the first trade and $-13$ on the second

hints.text: Buy on day 1. Does day 3 reach the take profit?
"At least 5%" includes equality, so day 3 sells at 252.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace each day and check the rules in order.

byKey.sameday: You let the bot buy 236 on day 6, the day it sold. It must wait, and day 7 is not a fall.
byKey.strict: You needed more than 5%. The rule is `>=`, so 252 against 240 sells on day 3.
byKey.first: You stopped after the first trade. Day 4's 249 is below 252, so the bot buys again.

explain.text: Day 3 sells at exactly 5% up, for $+12$. Day 4 buys 249, and day 6's 236 is at least 3% down, for $-13$. Day 7 cannot buy: 240 is not below 236.

screens.title: Tests before code
screens.prose: You have 40 minutes for this question in an assessment. The hidden tests are not shown, only their number. `contests/l15-debugging-under-time` showed how slow it is to debug without an expected answer.

params.title: The statement
lines: A bot trades one unit of one stock. Prices are whole pence.
It starts flat. Day 0 never trades.
While flat on day i >= 1, it buys at that day's price
when the price is below the previous day's price.
While long, it checks three rules on each later day, in order:
1. Sell if 100 * p >= 105 * entry (at least 5% up).
2. Sell if 100 * p <= 97 * entry (at least 3% down).
3. Sell if i - bought == 3 (held exactly 3 days).
A bot that sells on day i does not buy on day i.
If it still holds at the end, it sells at the last price.

screens.question: What do you do first?

options.text: Write two hand traces, one with a same-day sale
Code the rules, then run them on the 40-day file
options.why: You would get 249 and have no way to know it is right. A hand trace gives an answer to compare against.

options.text: Submit the starter to see which tests fail
options.why: The starter fails every test, which tells you nothing about the rules.

options.text: Code all three rules as separate functions first
options.why: Structure does not catch a wrong order of checks. A trace with known results does.

hints.text: How will you know your output is right?
You need expected values you worked out without the code.
Two hand traces: one simple, and one where a rule fires on a day with a fall, such as `[100, 95, 90, 85]`.

feedback.correct: Two traces with known answers catch most rule-order mistakes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need a way to tell a right answer from a wrong one.

byKey.b: You trusted the big file. Its answer means nothing until a small case is known to be right.
byKey.c: You used the starter as a test. It fails everything, so it shows nothing.
byKey.d: You started on structure. A wrong order of checks still passes a structure review.

explain.text: A hand trace is a test with a known answer. The trap list `[100, 95, 90, 85]` catches the same-day buy, and the hook list checks the take profit. Run both before the hidden tests.

ideas: List the state, the events and the order of checks before writing code.
Edge rules decide the answer. Watch day 0, a same-day sale and buy, an exact threshold and the last day.
Hand-trace two short inputs first, so the hidden tests have something to be compared against.

formula.name: A simulation
formula.note: One function applies one event; the checks inside follow the statement's order.

summary.trap: Letting the bot buy on the day it sold turns `[-5, 2]` into `[-10, 3]` on `[100, 95, 90, 85]`.

quiz.question: The bot bought at 200 on day 2. On day 5 the price is 194. Which rule sells it?

options.text: Rule 2, the stop: $19{,}400 \le 97 \times 200$
Rule 3, the time rule
options.why: Rule 3 is true too, but rule 2 comes first in the order and is true.

options.text: None: 194 is exactly 3% down, not more
options.why: "At most 3% below" includes 3% exactly: $19{,}400 \le 19{,}400$.

options.text: Rule 1, the take profit
options.why: 194 is below the entry, so rule 1 is false.

feedback.correct: Rule 2 is the first true rule in order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the rules in order, with equality.

explain.text: Rule 1 is false. Rule 2 holds with equality, $19{,}400 \le 19{,}400$, so it sells before rule 3 is checked.

quiz.question: The bot sells on day 4 at 95, and 95 is below day 3's price. What does it do next on day 4?

options.text: Nothing: it cannot buy on the day it sold
It buys at 95
options.why: You let the bot buy on the day it sold. The statement forbids it.

options.text: It buys on day 4 only if 95 is a new low
options.why: No such rule exists. The same-day rule forbids any buy on day 4.

options.text: It sells again
options.why: It holds one unit, which is already sold.

feedback.correct: It waits until day 5 at the earliest.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the same-day rule again.

explain.text: The statement says a bot that sells on day `i` does not buy on day `i`. The `else` on `long_` enforces it.

quiz.question: `strategy_from_file` reads a file with the header and no rows. What does it return?

options.text: It raises `IndexError`
options.why: `prices[-1]` is read only when the bot still holds, and with no prices it never buys.
No trade happened, so the count is 0.

options.text: It raises `KeyError` for `price_pence`
options.why: The header is there, so the key exists. There are just no rows.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow an empty list through `run_strategy`.

explain.text: `DictReader` yields no rows, so `load_prices` returns `[]`. The loop never runs and the end rule is skipped. The result is `[0, 0]`.

quiz.question: What total profit, in pence, does the bot make on `[100, 97, 99, 102, 101]`?

widget.label: Profit
widget.accept: 5: buy 97 and sell 102 on day 3, then buy 101 and sell it at 101

feedback.correct: $+5$ on the first trade and 0 on the second.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace each day and check the rules in order.

byKey.held: You held 97 to the end, at 101. Day 3's 102 is at least 5% up: $10{,}200 \ge 10{,}185$.
byKey.one: You bought at 100 on day 0. Day 0 never trades.

explain.text: Day 1 buys 97. Day 3's $10{,}200 \ge 105 \times 97 = 10{,}185$ sells for $+5$. Day 4 buys 101, which the end sells at 101.
